parole.testo: Denominal. From Aramaic אַבְזָרָא (ʾaḇzārā), ultimately from Middle Iranian; compare modern Persian ابزار (abzâr).

parole.significato: Forming words pertaining to population, inhabiting.
parole.testo: Back-formation from אוכלוסין / אֻכְלוּסִין (ukhlusín, “population”) or equivalently אוכלוסייה / אֻכְלוּסִיָּה (ukhlusiyá), from Aramaic אוכלוסין, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὄχλος (ókhlos).
Denominal from Aramaic אתרא. Compare Akkadian 𒆠 (ašrum), Arabic أَثَر (ʔaṯar), Ge'ez አሰር (ʾäsär).

parole.significato: father (a male parent, especially of a human; a male who parents a child (which he has sired, adopted, fostered, etc.))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic אַבָּא (ʾabbā). Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *ʾab-. Doublet of אָב ('áv), which is inherited.
Borrowed from Aramaic אַבְזָרָא (ʾaḇzārā), אֲבִזְרָא ('aḇizrā), אֲבִיזְרָא (ʾaḇizrā).
Borrowed from Aramaic גּוֹזָא (gōzā), אמגוזא, from unattested Old Persian *angauza, see Old Armenian ընկոյզ (ənkoyz) for more.
From Aramaic אדרא . Compare Classical Syriac ܐܕܪܐ (ʾāḏrā).
From Aramaic ארדיכלא, from Akkadian 𒀵𒂍𒃲 (arad ēkalli, “slave of the palace”). Cognate with Classical Syriac ܐܪܕܝܟܠܐ (ʾardēḵlāʾ).
From Aramaic אוכלוסין, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὄχλος (ókhlos).

parole.significato: A studio, such as a recording studio or television studio.
parole.testo: From Aramaic אולפן (ʾulpān, “learning”) / אוּלְפָּנָא, taken from בית אולפן (bēṯ ʾulpān, “schoolhouse”, literally “house of learning”). Doublet of אולפנה / אֻלְפָּנָה.
Borrowed from Aramaic אוּמָּנָא (ʾūmmānā, “artist, artisan, craftsman”) (Classical Syriac ܐܽܘܡܳܢܳܐ), from Akkadian 𒌝𒈪𒀀 (UM.MI.A /⁠ʾummānu⁠/, “expert, artisan, artist, craftsman, foreman”).
Borrowed from Aramaic אוקינוס, from Ancient Greek ὠκεανός (ōkeanós, “ocean”), from Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós, “Oceanus”).

parole.significato: the Ushpizin; the seven guests who spiritually visit the sukkah during Sukkot
parole.testo: From Aramaic, plural of אוּשְׁפִּיזָּא (ʾušpizzā, “lodging place, landlord, guest”), from Persian سپنج (sepanj).
Perhaps borrowed from Aramaic אִגַּרְתָּא (ʾiggartā). Cognates exist in many Semitic languages. The ultimate origin may be Iranian (compare Persian انگاره (engâre)).

parole.significato: barren woman, woman physically unable to bear children
parole.testo: From אַיִל (áyil, “ram”) + ־נִית (-nít), a diminutive suffix; from Aramaic ־נִיתָא, Classical Syriac -ܢܝܬܐ (-nīṯā).

parole.significato: onward, forth; in a specified direction
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic; ultimately from the root ה־ל־ך (h-l-k).
Borrowed from Aramaic אִילָנָא / ܐܺܝܠܳܢܳܐ (ʾīlānā, “tree”). Doublet of אֵלוֹן (elōn, “great tree”) and אַלּוֹן (allōn, “great tree; oak”).

parole.significato: No one is enforcing law and order (literally, "there is no law and there is no judge").
parole.testo: Calque of Aramaic לֵית דִּין וְלֵית דַּיָּן (“there is no law and there is no judge”) from Leviticus Rabbah 28:1 and Jerusalem Talmud.

parole.significato: where there's smoke, there's fire, there is a real cause for ambiance and rumors (literally, "there is no smoke without…
parole.testo: Middle ages: via Aramaic [Term?] from Latin flamma fumo est proxima, from a play by Plautus, 2nd century B.C.E.
From Aramaic איפכא מסתברא (“the opposite turns out”).

parole.significato: stretcher (a simple litter designed to carry a sick, injured, or dead person)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic *אֲלַנְקֵי /אֲלוּנְקֵי (“poles used to carry burdens on the shoulder of two or more persons”).
Borrowed from Aramaic אִמָּא (ʾimmā).

parole.significato: One of the Amoraim, sages of the Gemara.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic אֲמוֹרָא (“speaker”).
From Aramaic אֲמַתְלָא.

Borrowed from Aramaic אַסְפַּסְתָּא (ʾaspastā) / ܐܰܣܦܷܣܬܳܐ (ʾaspestā, “lucerne”), from Akkadian 𒊍𒉺𒊍𒋾 (aspastu, “presumably lucerne”), from Old Median *aspāstiš (“lucerne”), from Proto-Iranian *HacwaHastiš (“lucerne”, literally “horse-food”) from Proto-Iranian *Hácwah (“horse”) + Proto-Indo-European
Derived from Aramaic אַפּוֹטְרוֹפּוֹס, from Ancient Greek ἐπίτροπος (epítropos, “trustee, guardian”).
From Aramaic [Term?]. Related to קרא and קרה (“happen”).

Derived from Aramaic אֲשׁוּנָא (ʾăšūnā), אָשׁוּן (ʾāšūn, “hard”), where original ח (ḥ) or ע (ʿ) was replaced by א (ʾ) in one of the dialects, where א (ʾ), ח (ḥ), ע (ʿ) (and sometimes ה (h)) all merge to the same sound. Compare the alternative form, עָשׁוּן ('ashún). The same also happened in Samarit

parole.significato: last year (in the year before this one)
parole.testo: From Aramaic ܐܫܬܩܕܝ.
Back-formation from הִתְגָּרָה, from גרה, from Aramaic.

parole.significato: Etnachta, a first/kesar level disjunctive accent
parole.testo: From Aramaic אֶתְנַחְתָּא (ʾeṯnaḥtā), from a root meaning "to rest (i.e. to rest/stop reciting)".
According to Klein, from Aramaic בּֽדַח.

Borrowed from Aramaic בָּזִיכָא (bāzīḵā, “censer”), itself from Middle Iranian *bāžak (“cup”), ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂g- (“to distribute, allot”). Cognate with Old Armenian բաժակ (bažak, “cup, glass, mug”).
From Aramaic סגי נהור (“blind person”, literally “much light”).
From Aramaic בְּעַט (bəʿaṭ).
Presumably borrowed from Aramaic [Term?].
From Aramaic בַּר (bar), singular construct form of בְּרָא (bərā, “son”). Doublet of בֵּן (bēn).

parole.significato: May it not happen to us.
parole.testo: From Aramaic, meaning “outside of us”. The noun is first attested in writings of the twelfth or thirteenth century; the interjection derives from the noun.
From Biblical Aramaic בְּרַם.
Borrowed from Aramaic בָּתַר (bāṯar).
From Aramaic גַּדָּא.
According to Even-Shoshan, based on Aramaic גִּידְמָא דְדִיקְלָא, Gittin 37.

From Aramaic גושפנקא, from Middle Persian [script needed] (angustbān, “finger-guard; ring seal”), from Old Persian *anguštapāna, a compound of *angušta (“finger”) (see *Hangúštʰas) + *-pānah (“protector; guard”) (see *-paHā); compare Persian انگشتانه (angoštāne, “thimble”).
From Aramaic גזוזטרא, from Ancient Greek ἐξώστρα (exṓstra).
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda from Aramaic גְּלִידָא (glidá, “ice, frost”), and phono-semantic matching of Italian gelato (“ice cream”). Matching the pattern of לְבִיבָה (l'vivá) used for foods.

Compare Ugaritic 𐎂𐎌𐎎 (gšm, “rain, downpour”) and Arabic سَجَم (sajam, “water, tear”). The sense "body" (and, by extension, "substance") is first attested in Aramaic parts of the Book of Daniel and later gained currency in Medieval Hebrew. This sense appears to represent a borrowing from Aramaic, for

parole.significato: Introduces a subordinate clause, that, which, who
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic דְּ־ (də-), from earlier Aramaic דִּי (dī). Doublet of זֶה (this).

parole.significato: (usually in regard to a mitzvah or a law) biblical, Pentateuchal, derived or deriving authority directly from Biblical…
parole.testo: From Aramaic דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא, from דְּ־ (“of, from”) + אוֹרָיְתָא (“Torah”).

parole.significato: Then, then-, at that time: used with a noun phrase denoting a role, to clarify that the referent held the role at the t…
parole.testo: From Aramaic [Term?].

parole.significato: an example, a sample, a specimen
parole.testo: From Aramaic דּוּגְמָא (dūḡmāʾ), from Ancient Greek δεῖγμα (deîgma), from the verb δείχνω (deíchno, “to point”).
From Aramaic דווקא (dawqā, “exactness”).

Borrowed during the revival of Hebrew from Aramaic דּוּלְבָּא (plane), from whence also Arabic دُلْب (dulb) originates. It semantically replaced earlier עַרְמוֹן (armón), whose meaning had been obscured when Hebrew ceased to be spoken.

parole.significato: the wise need only a hint
parole.testo: Aramaic, lit. "[with] a hint is enough for a wise one".
From Aramaic דְּיוּתָא (dyōṯā).

Mishnaic: possibly via Aramaic דפתרא / ܕܦܬܪܐ (dptrʾ, “hide; account book”), from Ancient Greek διφθέρα (diphthéra, “prepared hide, piece of leather; anything made of leather”). Compare with Arabic دَفْتَر (daftar, “register; notebook”)

parole.significato: Darga, a type of conjunctive accent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic דַּרְגָּא (dargā, “step”). See also דֶּרֶג.

Borrowed from the Aramaic דרדס into the plural form דַּרְדָּסִין (dardásin), for translating the German Strümpfe, in the mid-19th century. A more recent learned borrowing from Aramaic דרדס, for the Hebrew version of the The smurfs in 1983, with the plural דַּרְדָּסִים (dardásim). The choice was expl
From Aramaic הא.
Denominated from Aramaic אַרְקָא (ʾarqā, “earth, land”), variant of אַרְעָא (ʾarʿā), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔarṣ́-. Doublet of אֶרֶץ.
Borrowed from Aramaic הֲדָדֵי.

parole.significato: to be grounded, to be earthed
parole.testo: Denominated from Aramaic אַרְקָא (ʾarqā, “earth, land”), variant of אַרְעָא (ʾarʿā), inherited from Proto-Semitic *ʔarṣ́-. Doublet of אֶרֶץ.
Borrowed from Aramaic הילכך (hilkákh).
From Aramaic אֲרֵי (ăre, “because, since, that”)
Borrowed from Aramaic זוּזָא (zūzā).

parole.significato: a trifle, minor thing, a triviality
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic זוּטָא.
From Aramaic.
From Aramaic זִימָא.
Used in the Talmud. Borrowed from Aramaic זיקוקין דנור, from זיקוקין (“sparks”) + דְּ־ (“of”) + נור (“fire”).
Borrowed from Aramaic 𐡆𐡌𐡍𐡀 (zmnʾ), from Old Persian *jamānā (“time”) (compare modern Persian زمان).
Via Aramaic זנא / זנה / ܙܢܐ descending from Proto-Iranian *jánHah, Proto-Indo-Iranian *ȷ́ánHas.

Borrowed from Aramaic חָבִיתָא (ḥāḇīṯā, “jug, amphora”), as are also Arabic خَابِيَة (ḵābiya) and Ge'ez ኅበይ, ሕበይ (ḫəbäy, ḥəbäy), ultimately from Akkadian 𒂁𒉺𒅁𒌉 (ḫābû, ḫāpû, “jug, amphora”) of obscure origin.
From Aramaic חֲבַל (ḥăḇal, “to damage, injure, destroy, travail”).
From Aramaic חברותא.
From Aramaic חד, which is cognate with Hebrew אֶחָד (ekhád, “one”).
From Aramaic חוֹפָא (ḥōfā, “border, rim”). Cognate with Arabic حَافَة (ḥāfa).
From Aramaic חוצפא (ḥuṣpāʾ, “audacity”).
Borrowed from Aramaic חָנוּתָא (ḥānūṯā).

parole.significato: lettuce (an edible plant, Lactuca sativa and its close relatives, having a head of green or purple leaves)
parole.testo: From Aramaic חַסָּא (khassaʾ). Compare likely cognates Arabic خَسّ (ḵass) and Maltese ħassa, both with the same meaning.
From Aramaic טֻפְרָא (ṭuprā, “nail, claw”).

parole.significato: draft (early version of a written work)
parole.testo: In קְטוּלָה pattern. From Aramaic טִיוּטָא, from the root ט־י־ט (“relating to deleting”).
From Aramaic טִינָא (ṭînāʾ, “mud, clay”).

parole.significato: tallit (a traditional Jewish prayer shawl with tassels which covers the chest and upper part of the back)
parole.testo: Unclear. Suggestions include: * From the Aramaic root ט־ל־ל (t-l-l) (related to the Hebrew root צ־ל־ל (ts-l-l); compare צל (tsél)). * From Ancient Greek στολή (stolḗ, “garment”).
Borrowed from Aramaic, literally, "may he straighten your strength".

parole.significato: wall: a structure serving as the exterior or a divider of a larger structure
parole.testo: Uncertain, theories include: * Borrowed from Aramaic כּוּתְלָא/ܟܘܬܠܐ, itself borrowed from Akkadian 𒄘𒋻 (/⁠kutallu⁠/, “behind, back of the head, backside, rear part of a structure”). * From Hittite [Term?] (/⁠kutt-⁠/, “wall”) + אֵל (el, “God, El, deity”).

Coined by the Academy of the Hebrew Language in 1912, from Aramaic כַּלָּנִיתָא (kallānīṯā, “type of reed”), based on ܟܠܘܢܝܬܐ (kallōnīṯā, “anemone”), both apparent diminutives of כַּלְּתָא (kalləṯā, “bride”). Can be synchronically analyzed as כַּלָּה (kalá, “bride”) + ־ָן (-án) + ־ִית (-ít).
From Aramaic כַּמֹּונָֹא / ܩܰܡܽܘܢܳܐ (kammōnā, “cumin”), from Akkadian 𒂵𒈬𒉡 (Ú.GAMUN /⁠kamūnu⁠/, “cumin”). Compare Ge'ez ከሚን (kämin), ካሚን (kamin), Arabic كَمُّون (kammūn).

parole.significato: a gang, a band (often with a negative connotation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic כְּנוּפְיָא /כִּינוּפְיָא (“crowd, assembly”), from כְּנַף (“to crowd, to gather”, verb).
From Aramaic כַּרְשָׁא (karšā), cognate with Arabic قِرْش (qirš).
Almost certainly an Aramaicism, from Aramaic כְּתָבָא. Cognate with Arabic كِتَاب (kitāb).
Borrowed from Aramaic כתיב (kṯiḇ, “written”), doublet of כתוב (katuv, “written”)

parole.significato: About, regarding, in connection with, with respect to.
parole.testo: From לְ־ (l'-) + גַּבֵּי (gabé), literally “to the backs of”. A calque of Aramaic [Term?]. First attested in the Talmud.
Aramaic [Term?]
Presumably borrowed from Aramaic לית בררה
Borrowed from Aramaic מאי.
Likely borrowed from Aramaic מְדִינְתָּא (məḏīntā), itself formed from the root of דין (“to judge”), denoting the place where judgement takes place. Cognate with Arabic مَدِينَة (madīna, “city”).

parole.significato: science (the collective discipline of study or learning acquired through the scientific method; the sum of knowledge ga…
parole.testo: *From Aramaic מנדע (“knowledge”)
Possibly borrowed from Aramaic מְהַל (“to circumcise”) and related to מָל (mal).
From Aramaic מוּט (mut, “to totter, stagger”).

Not conclusively known. The name, which was a personal epithet of Judah Maccabee and not an inherited surname, may derive from the Aramaic [script needed] (makkaba, “hammer”), in reference to Judas’s ferocity in battle. Conversely, the traditional Jewish explanation is that מַכַּבִּי (makkabbī) is a

parole.significato: from the outset, from the beginning
parole.testo: Presumably borrowed from Aramaic [Term?].

parole.significato: paroxytone; on the penult, stressed or accented on the second-to-last syllable
parole.testo: From Aramaic מִלְּעֵיל (milʿēl, “from above”), from מִן (min, “from”) + לְעֵיל (ləʿēl, “above”).

parole.significato: oxytone; on the ult, stressed or accented on the last syllable
parole.testo: From Aramaic מִלְּרַע (milraʿ, “from below”), from מִן (min, “from”) + לְרַע (ləraʿ, “below”), the latter from לְ־ (lə-, “to”) + אֲרַע (ʾăraʿ, “ground”).

parole.significato: nail (a spike-shaped metal fastener used for joining wood or similar materials)
parole.testo: Spelling borrowed from Aramaic מַסְמְרָא (masmərā, “pin, nail”). Cognate with Arabic مِسْمَار (mismār).

parole.significato: conclusion (decision or notion resulting from reflection)
parole.testo: From Aramaic מַסְקָנָא.

parole.significato: Mister (a title of respect for a man, preceding his surname in Modern Hebrew)
parole.testo: From Aramaic מרא (maraʾ); compare Classical Syriac ܡܪܐ (mārā). Perhaps reinforced by English Mr.

Borrowed from Aramaic מַשְׁכַּנְתָּא (mashkantá, “mortgaging”), a cognate of Classical Syriac ܡܫܟܢܐ (meškānā, “pledge”). Both of them are in turn borrowed from Akkadian maškānum (“dwelling place, deposit”).
Formed by applying the Hebrew pattern מְקֻטָּל (“-gon”) to the Aramaic borrowing תְּמַנְיָא (tmanya, “eight”).

parole.significato: Real estate: property consisting of land, buildings, etc.
parole.testo: An abbreviation of Aramaic נִכְסֵי דְלָא נָייְדֵי (nikhsé d'lá nay'dé, “non-mobile properties”).
Borrowed from Aramaic נְהַר (nəhar, “to shine”), whose root is related to Hebrew נ־ו־ר, whence words such נֵר (ner, “candle”) and מְנוֹרָה (m'norá, “menorah”) are derived.

Borrowed from Aramaic נַוְולָא (nawlā, “loom”), a Middle Iranian word continued in Persian نول (nôl, “the outer part of the mouth; a beak, bill; a spout; the neck of a bottle; tube, channel; anything on which one leans or is supported; a whirlpool, vortex”), ultimately from Old Tamil 𑀦𑀽𑀮𑁆 (nūl).

parole.significato: fish, found mostly in compounds to form names of sea creatures.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic נוּנָא (nūnā, “fish”), ultimately possibly from Akkadian 𒄩 (nūnum), possibly from Sumerian.

Borrowed from Aramaic נזר (literally “he abstained”), compare Arabic نَذَرَ (naḏara, literally “he consecrated”) and Arabic نَذِرَ (naḏira, literally “he showed reserve”), Akkadian 𒈾𒉌𒌓𒊒 (nazáru, literally “he cursed”).
From Aramaic נִסְיוֹנָא, forming the root נ־ס־ה (n-s-h).
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda from Aramaic נוּקָנִיקָה and Arabic نقانق (naqāniq). Ultimately from Latin lūcānica, through Byzantine Greek λουκάνικα (loukánika).

parole.significato: to become black, to become brown
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Aramaic אוּכָּמָא ('ūkkāmā, “black”). Cognate with Hebrew אוכמנית (ukhmanít, “blueberry”) and Classical Syriac ܐܘܟܡܐ ('ukkāmā, “black, sunburnt”).

parole.significato: An elderly man; an aged or old man.
parole.testo: From Aramaic סָבא (sāƀā) "ancestor; elder; grandfather"; related to native Hebrew שָׂב (sav).
Borrowed from Aramaic סָבְתָא.

parole.significato: segol (a Hebrew niqqud diacritical mark (ִ◌ֶ) in the form of three dots arranged as an upside-down triangle, pronounced…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic סְגוֹלָא / ܣܓܘܿܠܵܐ (sḡōlā, “cluster”), due to its graphic shape thought to resemble grapes. Accordingly, in the earliest Hebrew-language Masoretic treatises with shva on the samekh. Doublet of אֶשְׁכּוֹל (eshkól).
Borrowed from Aramaic סַגִּי. Cognate with Hebrew שַׂגִּיא. Compare שׂ־ג־ה (s-g-h).

parole.significato: A shop, a workshop: a small room for manufacturing or light industrial work.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic סַדְנָא m (saḏnā, “foundation”), identical to סַדָּן (sadán, “anvil”).
From Aramaic סוֹף (sōp̄)

parole.significato: restriction, a protective condition, fence, safeguard
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic סִיָגָא / ܣܝܓܐ (səyāḡā, literally “fence”), as is Arabic سِيَاج (siyāj, “fence”).

Borrowed from Aramaic סִיגְלָא (“an aromatic plant not definitively identified”), associated with violet based on Rashi's commentary about Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat, section 50.2, ״סגלי – עשב שקורין ויאו״ל״.
Borrowed from Aramaic סַכִּין (sakkīn), סַכִּינָא (sakkīnā), as is Arabic سِكِّين (sikkīn) and سِكِّينة (sikkīna).
Probably from Aramaic [Term?], saphel of מרט with partial reduplication.
Borrowed from Aramaic סְפינִתָּא (sǝp̄īntā), from whence also Arabic سَفِينَة (safīna, “ship, vessel”) was taken.

The spelling with ס in place of שׂ is either borrowed or influenced by Aramaic. Compare native Hebrew שָׂרַט (sarát/śāraṭ, “to scratch, gash, cut”) and שָׂרֶטֶת (sarétet/śāréṭeṯ, “a scratch, gash, cut, abrasion”). Cognate with Arabic شَرِيط (šarīṭ).

parole.significato: thick bearded, possessing a thick beard
parole.testo: From Aramaic עַב דְּקַן (ʿaḇ dəqan, “thick beard”).
From Aramaic עַדּי (ʿadī, “concieve, become pregnant”).
Borrowed from Aramaic עֲרִיק.

From Aramaic עַרְסָלָא/אַרְסָלָא collateral form of עַרְזָלָא/אַרְזָלָא, of disputed etymology, theories include: * From (possibly a diminutive form, see Jastrow) עַרְסָא (“bed”). * From עֲזַל (“to spin yarn”).
From Aramaic עַתִּיק (ʿattīq).
Borrowed from Aramaic פּוּרְעָנוּתָא.
Back-formation from Aramaic פְּסַנְתֵּרִין (p'santerín), with the ־ִין (-ín) reanalyzed as a plural ending, from Ancient Greek ψαλτήριον (psaltḗrion, “harp”).
From Aramaic פַּרְדֵּיסָא (pardēsā) (absolutive: פַּרְדֵּס (pardēs)), an Iranian borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Iranian *paridayjah.
From Aramaic פתגמא (piṯḡāmā), from Middle Persian 𐭯𐭢𐭲𐭠𐭬 (pgtʾm /⁠paygām, *pagtām⁠/). Compare Persian پیغام (peyġâm).

parole.significato: cobra, snake of the family Elapidae
parole.testo: From Aramaic פִּתְנָא (piṯnā), from Proto-Semitic *baṯan-.
Borrowed from Aramaic צִיפָא.
From Aramaic צלופחא.
Borrowed from Aramaic צַפְרָא טָבָא (ṣap̄rā ṭāḇā).
Derived from Aramaic קָאְקָא (ḳāʾḳā, “goose”), which is onomatopoeic in origin. Compare Arabic قاق (qāq, “raven”).
From Aramaic קַדִּישׁ (qaddīš, “holy”).

parole.significato: A box or other container or receptacle for storage or transport.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Aramaic קוּפְסָא (qup̄sā), from Ancient Greek κάψα (kápsa), from Latin capsa.

parole.testo: From the root ק־ב־ץ (k-b-ts), relating to gathering, collections, contractions. Cognates include Ugaritic 𐎖𐎁𐎕 (qbṣ, “tribe”) and Aramaic קיבוץ (qybwṣ) from which it might have been borrowed. Appears in the Dead Sea Scrolls. From Aramaic קַיְטָא (qayṭā, “summer”), compare native קַיִץ (káyits, qáyiṣ).

Considered borrowed from a predecessor of the later Aramaic קֻפְדָּא / קוּפְדָּא (qup̄dā), as well as Arabic قُنْفُذ (qunfuḏ), while the meaning of an owl well has a different identity; see the Arabic for more.

parole.significato: key (part of a piano or musical keyboard)
parole.testo: Aramaic קְלִידָא (qəlīḏā), from Ancient Greek κλείς (kleís).

parole.significato: practice what you preach, actions speak louder than words
parole.testo: Aramaic, (lit.) the reader/proclaimer of the letter, let him be [it's] messenger. Recorded multiple times in the Talmud.
From Aramaic קרפדאי.
From Aramaic קֻרְפְּדַאי (qurp'dai, “unknown creeping animal”), a phono-semantic matching of French crapaud (“toad”).
Borrowed in Medieval Hebrew from Aramaic קַרְקַפְתָּא (“head, skull”), with the meaning being curtailed to "scalp" in Modern Hebrew.
Borrowed from Aramaic רַמְשָׁא טָבָא (ramšā ṭāḇā).
Acronym, originally for Aramaic ריש מתיבתא (“head of yeshiva”).

Borrowed from Aramaic ܫܒܱܛܒܳܛܳܐ (šəḇaṭbāṭā), doublet of native forms שְׁבַצְבָּץ (shvatzbatz), שְׁבַצְבּוּץ (shvatzbutz), and בִּצְבוּץ (bitzbutz), ultimately a derivation of Proto-Semitic *būṣ- (“reed”).

parole.significato: Some, any; found chiefly in negative contexts, as well as questions and conditional constructs.
parole.testo: From Aramaic שֻׁם (šum), indefinite and construct form of שְׁמָא (š'mā, “name”). The determiner is an extension of the noun.

Ultimately from Old Aramaic שושמא (šūššmā), shortening of שומשומא (šumššemā), from Akkadian 𒃻𒈦𒌑𒈬 (/⁠šamaššammū⁠/), 𒊭𒈦𒌑𒈨 (/⁠šamaššammi⁠/, literally “oil plant”), compound of 𒉌 (/⁠šaman⁠/, “oil”) and 𒌑 (/⁠šammu⁠/, “plant”). Derived from Aramaic שיַרְתָּא (šyartā, “caravan”), which is from Arabic سَيَّارَة (sayyāra, “caravan”) or a similar term in a related language. Cognates are Classical Syriac ܫܝܪܬܐ (šyārtā, “caravan”), Palmyrene Aramaic 𐡵𐡩𐡴𐡶𐡠 (šyrtʾ, “caravan”).
From Aramaic שלדא.

parole.significato: blanket (a heavy, loosely woven fabric, usually large and woollen, used for warmth while sleeping or resting)
parole.testo: Perhaps from an unused verb in the root ס־מ־ך (s-m-k), alternatively borrowed from Aramaic מַשְׁכָּא.

Originally from Aramaic שִׁסְקָא, mentioned in the Talmud, the identification of which is unclear, although it was variously applied to the plum, almond or medlar by medieval commentators. The interpretation as medlar was adopted in the revival of Hebrew by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, which was subsequently

parole.significato: hour (a unit of time of one twenty-fourth of a day (sixty minutes))
parole.testo: From Aramaic שעתא (šāʿəṯā). Cognate with Arabic سَاعَة (sāʕa).
From Aramaic תַגָּא (“crown”).
From Aramaic ܬܘܬܐ/תותא (tūtā).
Borrowed from Aramaic תָּרֵץ (“to make straight; to harmonize”).
From Aramaic תלת, which is cognate with Hebrew שָׁלוֹשׁ (shalósh, “three”).
From Aramaic תלת (“three”). Also borrowed into Punic, transcribed in De materia medica 2:102 as τιτλώ, likely for *𐤕𐤋𐤕𐤀 (*tiltō).

parole.significato: date (the fruit of the date palm, Phoenix dactylifera, somewhat in the shape of an olive, containing a soft, sweet pulp…
parole.testo: An early borrowing from Aramaic תמרא (tamrā, tamrē, təmārā); cognate with Arabic ثَمَر (ṯamar, “fruit; crops”) and fellow borrowing تَمْر (tamr, “date”).

parole.significato: One of the Tannaim, sages of the Mishnah.
parole.testo: From Aramaic תנא.

parole.significato: Tanu Rabbanan (a common phrase in Judaism used before citing Baraita)
parole.testo: Derived from Aramaic תְּנוּ רַבָּנָן (tənû rabbānān, “Talmudic Baraita introduction”, literally “our teachers have taught”). The pronunciation of תְּנוּ as תָּנוּ is probably influenced by Hebrew שָׁנוּ.
From Aramaic תְּרֵיסַר (tərēsar).
From Aramaic תתא.

parole.significato: (archaic) a kind of vessel, basin, basket.
parole.testo: Etymology disputed. Many theories exist, the main ones being: * From Aramaic קרטל (qarṭāl, “basket”) (Syriac spelling ܩܪܛܠܐ) which itself could be from: ** Hittite 𒄑𒆳𒋫𒀀𒀠 (kurtal-, kartal-) ** Middle Persian glyw' (grīw, “a measure of grain, a peck”) + -dʾl (dār, “holder, keeper, container of”), or *
Either borrowed from Aramaic אִכָּרָא (“farmer”) or Akkadian 𒇽𒀳 (ikkarum); compare also Classical Syriac ܐܟܪܐ (ʾakkārā).

parole.significato: Related to announcing, preaching, declaring, proclaiming
parole.testo: From Aramaic כְּרַז / ܟܪܰܙ (kraz, “to preach”), from Ancient Greek κηρύσσειν (kērússein, “to preach”). Cf. Daniel 3:4 and 5:29. Alternatively, instead of Ancient Greek, it is also suggested it might be borrowed from Old Persian. Compare Ge'ez ከረዘ (käräzä) and Arabic كَرَزَ (karaza).

(village): From Aramaic כַּפְרָא / ܟܰܦܪܳܐ (kap̄rā, “village, open town, unfortified town”), from Akkadian 𒅗𒀊𒊒 (kapru, “farm, village; a settlement outside of a city”), considered to be from the non-Akkadian “Mari language”, that is it is formed either in the unknown East Semitic or the unknown Amori

parole.significato: Easter (a Christian feast commemorating the resurrection of Jesus Christ)
parole.testo: Likely a reborrowing from Aramaic פַּסְחָא (pasḥā) or Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha, “Passover”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew פֶּסַח (pésaḥ, “Passover”), which is a doublet.
